doc.title: Tony Marino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 25, 2025

title: Afro Blue video with Joe Wagner; drop-in markers
summary: The duo video with guitarist Joe Wagner and the practice of rhythmic markers to bring in the audience.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: So when folks eventually watch this video on our Fillius Jazz YouTube channel I’m going to suggest that they Google you and a fellow named Joe Wagner, guitar player?
And you were playing the tune “Afro Blue.”
Oh good. I don’t remember it that much but yeah.
You both were playing your instruments like they were drums for a while.
Oh, good. I like that, I like opening up that way.

Yeah. And then it was just very spontaneous and creative and every once in a while you getting back to that melody thing, you’d hop up to the melody and play [scats]. And it made for, like I don't know if there’s markers in music I think that help. If your mind is wandering all of a sudden someone plays something and you go ut – yeah. It sort of brings you back in.

We do that often. You know? Especially for drum solo when everything drops out and it’s just him. I mean I’m not talking about trading eights, I’m talking about whole song forms you know. So but we’ll drop in whatever little rhythmic entity there is to bring into the bridge or something, or it might be something at the end of the tune, and then we’ll just wait for that and we’ll hit it every time, just so that – I think it helps the audience too, to bring them into – we’re listening, we’re not chewing gum and running to the bar. I’ve had that happen to me too during bass solo, you know, where the horn players run to the bar and have a taste. And I’m done with my solo and there’s no one there to bring me out of it. That used to get me a little mad.
